title: Another 2p on dividend, savings and property income
headline: Another 2p, repeating Budget 2025. If it raises what the first did: £2.2bn.
description: Budget 2025 put 2 points on the tax rates for dividends (from April 2026) and for savings and property income (from April 2027). Do it again: a further 2 points on each. The Treasury certified what the first round raises; this assumes the second round raises the same, year by year, which nobody has costed.

baselinePolicy.text: Dividend rates +2 points from April 2026 (ordinary 10.75%, upper 35.75%); savings income +2 points at every rate and separate property income rates of 22%, 42% and 47% from April 2027 (Table 4.1 lines 49 to 51). Together they raise £2.2bn in 2029-30.
alreadyIncludes: Dividend, savings and property income tax rises (Budget 2025, Table 4.1 lines 49, 50, 51).

lines.title: Property Income: Introduce separate tax rates for property income at 22% for the property basic rate, 42% for the property higher rate and 47% for the property additional rate, from 6 April 2027
Dividend Income: Increase tax rates on dividend income by 2ppts at the ordinary and upper rate from 6 April 2026

Savings Income: Increase tax rates on savings income by 2ppts at the basic, higher and additional rate from 6 April 2027 and maintain the Starting Rate of Savings limit at £5000 from April 2026 to April 2031

rawSource.note: Repeat: the Treasury's certified costing for the first 2 points, taken as the yield of a second 2 points, year by year. Positive scorecard values reduce borrowing; here receipts positive means more revenue. Effects before the start year are not applied.

caveats: Nobody has costed a second 2 points. This assumes it raises exactly what the Treasury costed for the first; in practice a higher rate brings a larger behavioural response (more incorporation, more use of ISAs and pensions, more dividends deferred), so the true yield would be somewhat lower.
The Treasury's costing is on the OBR November 2025 forecast, not the March 2026 baseline used here; the difference is small relative to the figures.

considerations.text: The first 2 points came with the Treasury's and OBR's agreed behavioural response built in; a second 2 points on top would meet a larger one, because the gap to the rates on earnings and to tax-free wrappers widens. The figure here is the first round repeated, not a costing of the second.

Falls on people with dividends outside ISAs and pensions (company owner-managers above all), savers with interest above the personal savings allowance, and landlords. It does not touch earnings, so it stays outside the manifesto's tax lock as written.

interactions.text: Reversing the first 2 points and adding a second makes no sense together; the two cancel.
